## Proof

**Leak check:** The problem text contains only the problem statement and procedural constraints. No answer, solution sketch, or formalization notes are leaked. Proceeding.

**Key tool — Kummer's theorem.** For a prime $p$, the $p$-adic valuation $v_p\!\binom{2n}{n}$ equals the number of carries produced when adding $n$ and $n$ in base $p$. Hence $\binom{2n}{n}$ is **not** divisible by $11$ if and only if adding $n + n$ in base $11$ produces **no carries**.

**Carry-free condition.** Writing $n$ in base $11$ as $n = (d_k \dots d_1 d_0)_{11}$, the addition $n + n$ is carry-free exactly when every digit satisfies $2d_i < 11$, i.e. $d_i \le 5$. Thus

$$\binom{2n}{n}\not\equiv 0 \pmod{11} \iff \text{every base-11 digit of } n \text{ lies in } \{0,1,2,3,4,5\}.$$

**Range analysis.** Note $11^3 = 1331$, so
$$1330 = 11^3 - 1 = (10\;10\;10)_{11}.$$
Every integer $0 \le n \le 1330$ has at most three base-11 digits. Among these, the numbers whose base-11 digits all lie in $\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}$ range from $0$ up to
$$(5\;5\;5)_{11} = 5\cdot 121 + 5\cdot 11 + 5 = 665 < 1330.$$
So every such number automatically satisfies $n \le 1330$.

**Counting.** Each of the three digit positions independently takes one of $6$ values $\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}$, giving $6^3 = 216$ nonnegative integers (including $0$). Excluding $n = 0$ (we want **positive** integers), the count is

$$216 - 1 = \boxed{215}.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
